newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FOCUS-Aer Lingus 96 pretax profit soars.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Aer Lingus 96 pretax profit soars.

text.p: Ireland's Aer Lingus said on Wednesday that pre-tax profits soared by 130 percent to 40.9 million punts ($63.3 million) last year but warned that continued cost reductions were essential for future profitability.
The national airline said two non-trading factors contributed significantly to the sharp improvement in profit at the pre-tax level.

The net interest charge fell to 1.3 million in 1996 from 20.4 million a year earlier while the write-back of prior year provisions no longer required resulted in an exceptional contribution of 4.4 million, the airline said in a statement.
Aer Lingus also reported strong growth on all major route groups, a solid performance from its cargo division and an improving result for subsidiary companies.
Operating profit from continuing businesses, a key measure of the trading performance of the group, rose by four percent to 41.8 million punts while turnover was up nine percent at 766 million.
Chairman Bernie Cahill said the group made significant further progress last year but warned that the 1996 results were achieved during a period of considerable buoyancy.
It was widely accepted by sector analysts that the industry was probably at the top of its trade cycle, he said.
"It is clear that sustained effort is vital if we are to achieve the further cost reductions in unit costs which are an essential prerequisite to profitability," Cahill said.
The airline is also exploring the possibility of entering into a major strategic alliance.
"We have recognised for some time that alliances are important in the increasingly globalised industry in which the group operates," chief executive Gary McGann said.

"The considerably improved financial position of the group, coupled with the unambiguous focus on profitable expansion, enhances the prospects of identifying appropriate partners for the future," he said.
The group continued to strengthen its balance sheet last year and had a net cash balance of 38.7 million punts at end-December 1996 compared to net debt of 41.4 million a year earlier.
Shareholders' funds grew by 21 percent to 190.5 million as the financial position benefited from strong cashflow from operations and from the sale of non-core assets.
The disposals were undertaken as part of an EU-approved restructuring plan to rescue the debt-burdened airline and put it on a sound, commercial footing.

Under the terms of the plan, the Irish government gave the airline 175 million punts over a three-year period and in return Aer Lingus cut costs by shedding some 12 percent of its workforce and by disposing of non-core assets such as its hotel chain.
The government, Aer Lingus' main shareholder, welcomed the 1996 results.

"The early 1990s were difficult for the global aviation industry and Aer Lingus, like many other airlines, was compelled to restructure its operations in order to meet the challenges posed by a constantly changing market," Irish transport minister Alan Dukes said in a statement.
"That these challenges have been successfully met to date is amply demonstrated by the 1996 results which mirror the turnaround shown in recent years." ($ = 0.645 Irish Pounds)
